Human in the Loop: Interactive Passive Automata Learning
via Evidence-Driven State-Merging Algorithms
Christian A. Hammerschmidt 1 Radu State 1 Sicco V erwer2
Abstract
We present an interactive version of an evidence-
driven state-merging (EDSM) algorithm for
learning variants of ﬁnite state automata. Learn-
ing these automata often amounts to recovering
or reverse engineering the model generating the
data despite noisy, incomplete, or imperfectly
sampled data sources rather than optimizing a
purely numeric target function.
Domain expertise and human knowledge about
the target domain can guide this process, and
typically is captured in parameter settings. Of-
ten, domain expertise is subconscious and not ex-
pressed explicitly. Directly interacting with the
learning algorithm makes it easier to utilize this
knowledge effectively.
1. Introduction
Automata, and ﬁnite state machines in particular, have
long been a formal model used in computer science to de-
signing software and analyzing computer systems them-
selves ( Lee & Y annakakis, 1996). Our knowledge about
automata models comes from different source: Firstly, we
have studied formal systems in detail and understand them
as algebraic systems we can pose decision problems about.
Secondly, we have experience lots experience applying
them as a model language.
In learning, these tasks are done inversely to recover,
reverse-engineer, or understand an unknown data source,
typically a communication protocol or software controller .
The automata models themselves are also seen as suit-
able to gain epistemic insight into the system of interest
(Hammerschmidt et al., 2016; V aandrager, 2017) for hu-
mans beyond learning models that minimize a given error
function, or are used in model checkers for formal analysis.

title: Continuous Learning Based Novelty Aware Emotion Recognition System
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2306.08733v1
published: 2023-06-14T20:34:07Z
summary: Current works in human emotion recognition follow the traditional closed learning approach governed by rigid rules without any consideration of novelty. Classification models are trained on some collected datasets and expected to have the same data distribution in the real-world deployment. Due to the fluid and constantly changing nature of the world we live in, it is possible to have unexpected and novel sample distribution which can lead the model to fail. Hence, in this work, we propose a continuous learning based approach to deal with novelty in the automatic emotion recognition task.

Abstract
Against the backdrop of the replication crisis, quantitative research in human resource management, as in many areas of
the social sciences, relies on instruments and procedures whose legitimacy is often taken for granted. However, closer
examination of how data are produced, interpreted, and justiﬁed reveals a more complex and less unproblematic picture.
Drawing on a systematic review of 398 empirical articles, this paper shows how dominant methodological practices
become standardized and taken for granted, despite their well-documented limitations. Rather than treating these
practices as isolated methodological issues, the article argues that they are embedded in a broader epistemic regime in
which statistical tools contribute to the production of scientiﬁc legitimacy while simultaneously obscuring their own
limitations. In this perspective, practices such as the metric treatment of ordinal scales, the routine use of hypothesis
testing, and the reliance on non-probabilistic samples are not merely technical choices, but mechanisms through which a
performative form of rigor is constructed. The ﬁndings suggest that quantiﬁcation in HRM does not simply describe
phenomena, but actively shapes what can be observed, compared, and asserted. This calls for a more reﬂexive approach
to research methodology, attentive to the epistemic conditions under which knowledge claims are produced.

Against the backdrop of the replication crisis, quantitative research in human resource management, as in many areas of the social sciences, relies on instruments and procedures whose legitimacy is often taken for granted. However, closer examination of how data are produced, interpreted, and justified reveals a more complex and less unproblematic picture. Drawing on a systematic review of 398 empirical articles, this paper shows how dominant methodological practices become standardized and taken for granted, despite their well-documented limitations. Rather than treating these practices as isolated methodological issues, the article argues that they are embedded in a broader epistemic regime in which statistical tools contribute to the production of scientific legitimacy while simultaneously obscuring their own limitations. In this perspective, practices such as the metric treatment of ordinal scales, the routine use of hypothesis testing, and the reliance on non-probabilistic samples are not merely technical choices, but mechanisms through which a performative form of rigor is constructed. The findings suggest that quantification in HRM does not simply describe phenomena, but actively shapes what can be observed, compared, and asserted. This calls for a more reflexive approach to research methodology, attentive to the epistemic conditions under which knowledge claims are produced.
